title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
one_sentence_summary: A Vision Transformer turns an image into a sequence of patch tokens and processes them with transformer self-attention instead of convolution, making it a flexible vision backbone for supervised and self-supervised learning.
quick_recall: Split the image into patches, map each patch to a token, add position information and often a class token, then use transformer encoder blocks to mix information globally across all tokens.
big_picture: ViT reframes image understanding as sequence modeling. Rather than applying local convolutional filters repeatedly across a grid, it treats each image patch as a token and lets self-attention decide which patches should exchange information. This gives the model a flexible global communication mechanism and makes the internal representation compatible with token-based vision objectives.
why_it_exists: CNNs encode a strong locality and translation-bias prior, which is often useful, but it also constrains how information is combined. ViT exists to explore a simpler and more general alternative: represent an image as tokens and let the model learn relationships among all parts of the image directly. This is especially useful when the learning objective is expressed over tokens, global image summaries, or patch-level comparisons rather than hand-designed convolutional feature maps.
intuition: Think of an image as a set of puzzle pieces. A CNN scans nearby pixels with fixed-size filters, while a ViT first turns each puzzle piece into a token and then repeatedly asks, ‘Which other pieces matter to me?’ Self-attention is the mechanism that answers that question. A class token, when used, acts like a learnable summary slot that collects evidence from all patch tokens and becomes a global image representation.
core_explanation: ViT begins by splitting an image into non-overlapping patches, flattening each patch, and projecting it into a shared embedding space. Those embeddings form a token sequence. The sequence is then augmented with positional information so the model can recover spatial arrangement. Transformer encoder blocks process the tokens: each token can attend to every other token, mixing local and global information in a data-dependent way. After several blocks, either the class token or pooled patch tokens are used for prediction or representation learning. The key idea is that the image is no longer a 2D grid processed by convolution; it is a sequence processed by attention.
mechanism: 1) Patchify the image into a grid of fixed-size patches. 2) Convert each patch into a vector embedding with a learned linear projection. 3) Add positional embeddings so the model knows where each patch came from. 4) Run the resulting token sequence through repeated transformer encoder layers. Each layer typically contains multi-head self-attention and an MLP, with residual connections and normalization. 5) Read out a global representation, often from a class token, for classification or downstream use. In self-supervised settings, patch tokens and the class token can both participate in teacher-student matching or masked prediction, which is why ViT is not just a classifier backbone but a general token processor for vision.
ml_relevance: ViT is central to modern vision representation learning because it changes the unit of computation from convolutional feature maps to tokens. That makes it compatible with objectives that operate over token sequences, such as comparing teacher and student token embeddings, aggregating patch-level information, or applying masked-token training. In multimodal and self-supervised methods, ViT provides a clean interface between architecture and learning objective.
practical_example: Suppose you want a model to represent photos of animals for self-supervised pretraining. A ViT would split each photo into patches, encode each patch as a token, and use a class token to summarize the whole image. During training, two differently augmented views of the same image can be passed through teacher and student ViTs, and the model learns to produce compatible representations. The patch-token structure makes it easy to compare or align representations at the token level, while the class token provides a compact global descriptor for downstream classification or retrieval.

mathematical_foundation.overview: The mathematics of ViT is mostly the mathematics of tokenization plus self-attention. The important part is not the exact formulas themselves, but what they say about how an image becomes a sequence and how every token can influence every other token.

sections.title: Patch embedding
sections.explanation: An image is divided into patches, and each patch is mapped to a token vector. This is the bridge from pixels to sequence tokens.

equations.explanation: x is the input image. H and W are height and width, and C is the number of channels, such as 3 for RGB. This notation reminds us that ViT starts with an image tensor, not a sequence.

The image is split into N non-overlapping patches, each of side length P. Each patch is flattened into a vector of length P^2 C. This is the tokenization step: a 2D image becomes a 1D sequence of patch vectors.

Each flattened patch x_i is projected into an embedding vector z_i. Here E is a learned projection matrix and b is a bias term. The purpose is to put all patch tokens into the same feature space so the transformer can process them uniformly.

sections.title: Adding position information
sections.explanation: Because attention alone does not know patch order, positional embeddings inject spatial layout back into the token sequence.

equations.explanation: p_i is the positional embedding for the i-th patch token. Adding it to z_i tells the model where the patch came from in the image. Without this, the transformer would treat the patch sequence as a bag of tokens with no geometry.

sections.title: Self-attention
sections.explanation: Self-attention lets each token gather information from all other tokens in a content-dependent way. This is the core mechanism that replaces convolutional locality with global interaction.

equations.latex: Q = XW_Q,\quad K = XW_K,\quad V = XW_V
equations.explanation: X is the matrix of token embeddings stacked by row. Q, K, and V are query, key, and value matrices produced by learned linear maps W_Q, W_K, and W_V. Queries decide what a token is looking for, keys describe what each token offers, and values carry the information that gets aggregated.

This is scaled dot-product attention. QK^\top measures similarity between every query and every key, so each token can score all other tokens. The \sqrt{d_k} factor keeps the dot products numerically stable when the key dimension d_k is large. The softmax turns scores into weights that sum to 1, and multiplying by V forms a weighted average of information from other tokens. In vision, this is how distant patches can directly influence one another.

sections.title: Class token and global readout
sections.explanation: A learnable class token can collect information from all patch tokens and serve as a global summary of the image.

equations.explanation: x_{\mathrm{cls}} is the learnable class token, and the semicolon means concatenation into a single token sequence. This token is not tied to any patch; instead, it learns to absorb image-wide information during attention layers.

common_misconceptions: ViT does not mean ‘no inductive bias at all.’ It still has important biases from patch size, positional embeddings, architecture depth, and training objective.
A class token is not required for every ViT use case; some models pool patch tokens or use token-level heads instead.
Self-attention is not automatically better than convolution. ViT often needs careful training and enough data or strong regularization to match or beat CNNs in some settings.
Patch tokens are not the same as CNN feature maps. They are a sequence representation of the image, which changes how downstream objectives are formulated.
Global attention does not mean the model always uses all context equally; it learns which tokens matter for each query.
limitations: Patchifying can discard fine-grained spatial detail if patches are too large.
Self-attention can be computationally expensive because every token can interact with every other token.
ViT may be less data-efficient than CNNs when training from scratch on limited data.
Interpretability can still be challenging because attention weights are not a complete explanation of the model’s behavior.
The architecture alone does not guarantee good representations; the training objective and augmentation strategy matter a lot.
mental_models: Image-as-sentence: patches are words, positional embeddings are word order, and attention is cross-token context.
Class token as a learnable global scratchpad that collects evidence from the whole image.
Self-attention as content-based routing between patches.
ViT as a universal interface for vision objectives that operate on token sequences rather than on convolutional feature maps.

relationship_justifications.reason: CLIP commonly uses ViT as an image encoder, so the two topics are closely connected in multimodal representation learning.
ResNet is a major convolutional baseline commonly compared against ViT in vision representation learning.

deep_dive:
ViT can be understood as a change in representation layer, not just a change in model family. A CNN imposes locality directly in the computation: nearby pixels are combined first, and larger-scale structure emerges gradually through depth. ViT instead performs an explicit conversion from pixels to a sequence of patch tokens, then uses attention to decide where information should flow. This is a more flexible but less prescriptive prior.

The class token is particularly important in practice because it creates a dedicated location for a global summary to emerge. During self-attention, the class token can attend to all patches and be updated by them, while patch tokens can also influence one another. In supervised classification, the class token is often used as the final representation. In self-supervised methods, the same token can be used as the target for alignment between teacher and student networks, or as one of several views of the image representation.

A useful way to compare ViT and CNNs is to ask where spatial relations are encoded. In a CNN, translation equivariance and local receptive fields are built into the architecture. In ViT, those biases are weaker and more explicit: patch size, positional embeddings, and training objective all shape what spatial structure the model learns. This makes ViT very adaptable, but it also means performance is more dependent on optimization and data regime.

For DINO-style methods, the main advantage of ViT is that the architecture naturally exposes a sequence of tokens and a global summary token. That interface makes it easy to define objectives over token distributions or teacher-student similarity without translating everything through CNN feature maps. In other words, ViT is not just a different backbone; it is a different algebra for vision learning.
